core_summary: Introduces the fundamental concept of congruence of plane figures, specifically focusing on geometric symbols and triangles. It explores superimposition, rotation, and reflection, and defines corresponding vertices, sides, and angles. It examines the minimum criteria needed to establish triangle congruence (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) and establishes the strict convention for vertex order in congruence notation.
key_concepts: Congruence of Plane Figures (identical shape and size)
Corresponding Vertices, Corresponding Sides, and Corresponding Angles
Strict Vertex Correspondence in Congruence Notation (e.g., ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ)
Minimal Conditions for Triangle Congruence (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS)
Application of Congruence in Real-World Designs and Cardboard Cutouts

key_terms.definition: Geometric figures that have the exact same shape and size, matching perfectly when superimposed over each other.
Placing one geometric figure directly over another to check if they coincide completely.
Pairs of vertices from two congruent figures that align with each other upon superimposition.
Pairs of sides from two congruent figures that match in position and have equal lengths.
Pairs of angles from two congruent figures that match in position and have equal measures.
Side-Angle-Side congruence rule stating two triangles are congruent if two sides and the included angle of one equal those of the other.
Side-Side-Side congruence rule stating two triangles are congruent if all three sides of one equal the corresponding three sides of the other.
Angle-Side-Angle congruence rule stating two triangles are congruent if two angles and the included side of one equal those of the other.
Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side congruence rule for right-angled triangles.

key_takeaways: Two figures are congruent if they share identical shape and size, regardless of orientation (rotation or flip).
Congruence notation strictly preserves vertex mapping (e.g., ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ implies A corresponds to X, B to Y, C to Z).
Establishing triangle congruence requires testing minimal sets of measurements (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) rather than all six components.
Once congruence is proven, all corresponding sides and corresponding angles are guaranteed to be equal.
